newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-BHP SEES NO CASE TO FLOAT OIL ASSETS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BHP SEES NO CASE TO FLOAT OIL ASSETS.

text.p: Australian resources giant The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) on Friday made clear it was jealous of its oil assets but no longer fond of the man who ran them.

BHP managing director John Prescott told a news conference called to explain John O'Connor's shock resignation that the former Mobil Corp executive had fallen out with the board over a proposal to float off BHP's petroleum assets.
O'Connor, a board director himself, is said to have wanted them hived off to free the petroleum division from the fetters of a diversified giant like BHP, giving it free rein.
Prescott and the rest of the board did not.
"It's not a strategy that we totally reject; it's just at this time, for this particular set of assets, it's not in shareholders' best interests," Prescott said.
The petroleum division, the biggest contributor to BHP's profit, has in recent times also been the group's best hedge against weak commodity prices and a soft steel market.
"It is an important part of managing BHP's exposure to the commodity market," Prescott said.
The petroleum division, which boasts world-class assets like the Bass Strait and North West Shelf fields off the Australian coast, is also a big source of BHP's franking credits, he added.
These credits are earned by the company as it pays tax on earnings and can be passed onto shareholders with dividends. Shareholders can then use them to offset their own tax bill.
Prescott said on Friday the board had considered spinning off the petroleum divison from the rest of the group a few months ago but decided unanimously against it.
Asked if O'Connor himself had voted against the proposal, he said: "I think the 'whole' board is an unambiguous statement".

O'Connor has not commented about his dispute with the board, but his departure came hot on the heels of media reports that O'Connor was still arguing the case for a spin-off -- this time outside BHP, in briefings to share analysts.
"He obviously could not sell it (the idea) to the board and tried to sell it outside the group, and that's unacceptable at any time," said analyst Umit Safak, of broker HSBC James Capel.
BHP chairman Jerry Ellis confirmed as much on Friday.
"The recent events were the straw that broke the camel's back," he said.
But investors, not the board, had the final word on Friday.
BHP shares tumbled immediately after the announcent, closing 45 cents lower at A$16.99 and ending three days of managemnent tormoil which wiped about A$2 billion off its market value.
O'Connor's exit followed the sudden departures of minerals division chief Dick Carter and iron ore head Geoff Wedlock.
O'Connor, hired from Mobil a year ago in a rare case of outside recruitment for BHP, is seen as the biggest loss.

"They have got rid of the one guy who appeared to be the leading light there, the one businessman who appeared to be running his business in a very clean, efficient fashion," the head of an institutional dealing desk told Reuters.
"You'd think that the international perception would be that the company is in a state of shambles."
"The market is resoundingly saying 'get me out'," he added.
-- Melbourne bureau 613-9286-1421
